one_liner: Single-header, public-domain sprintf/snprintf replacement claiming 4-35x faster formatting than MSVC 2008's CRT.
what_it_does: stb_sprintf.h is a single-header reimplementation of the C sprintf/snprintf/vsprintf/vsnprintf family (stbsp_ prefixed functions), plus a callback-driven stbsp_vsprintfcb that streams output in STB_SPRINTF_MIN-sized chunks instead of building the whole string first. It covers the full CRT format surface (%d/%x/%f/%e/%g/%a/%n, both MSVC %I64d and GCC %lld/%jd/%zd length specifiers) plus extras standard sprintf lacks: thousands-separator commas (%'d), SI/JEDEC unit suffixes (%$d, %$$d), and binary output (%b). Include the header normally for declarations only; define STB_SPRINTF_IMPLEMENTATION in exactly one translation unit to get the code, per the standard STB single-file-library convention.
how_it_is_fast: It bypasses the CRT's generic, often locale-aware formatting machinery with hand-written, allocation-free integer/float-to-ASCII routines that feed a small internal buffer and a callback, so it never calls malloc and stays small enough to fit in cache (header states ~8K compiled with float support, ~4K without, vs. ~16K pulled in by MSVC's static sprintf). Float-to-string conversion uses an internal double-double (~105-bit) arithmetic scheme for round-trip-correct output without going through the CRT's arbitrary-precision or locale-sensitive dtoa path (documented in the header's FLOATS/DOUBLES section).
when_to_use: Game/graphics/embedded C or C++ codebases that want a small, dependency-free, single-header drop-in for heavy sprintf/snprintf call volume
Cross-platform code that wants one format-string dialect instead of juggling MSVC (%I64d) vs GCC (%lld) differences for 64-bit integers
Formatting-heavy hot paths (many floats/ints or long strings per frame/tick) where CRT sprintf throughput is a known bottleneck
Code-space-constrained targets (embedded, consoles) where ~8K of formatting code beats linking in a full CRT static sprintf (~16K per the header)
Want built-in thousands separators or SI/JEDEC-suffix number formatting (%'d, %$d, %$$d) without hand-rolling it
when_not_to_use: Strict C-standard sprintf conformance is required: open issues document divergent behavior for '+'/' '/'0' flags on unsigned types, negative width via '*', and %n with non-default size (issues #1788-#1790, #1785, #1778)

Format strings or precision values come from untrusted input: issue #1792 shows a buffer overrun via large integer precision (e.g. "%0.513x"), and issue #1963 shows stbsp_snprintf(buf, 0, ...) with a non-NULL buf writes one byte before the buffer -- both open, unpatched as of 2026-09-24
You rely on the common "call with count=0 to get required length" idiom against a non-NULL buffer pointer -- that exact pattern triggers the #1963 OOB write
You need independently benchmarked, modern numbers before committing: the header's speedup table is first-party, measured against MSVC 2008's CRT only, no CPU model or flags given (Tier C evidence)
16-bit int platforms are a target: issue #1779 is an open feature request, not currently supported

integration.dependencies: none (only <stdarg.h> and <stddef.h> from the C standard library)
integration.min_toolchain: C89/C99-compatible C or C++ compiler; no C++ standard required. Explicit shims for MSVC, GCC (>=4.8), and Clang (including ASan attribute handling)
integration.platforms: any (portable C; explicit 32-/64-bit pointer-size detection for x86, x86-64, aarch64, ppc64, s390x)
integration.thread_safety: Formatting calls themselves use only stack-local state per call (reentrant). stbsp_set_separators() mutates process-wide static globals (comma/period characters) with no locking, so it is not safe to call concurrently with formatting on other threads. Not explicitly documented as thread-safe by the author.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial -- explain: functions are stbsp_-prefixed, not sprintf/snprintf themselves (rename via STB_SPRINTF_DECORATE or #define if a literal drop-in is needed); stbsp_snprintf always null-terminates output, which the header notes differs from some CRT snprintf implementations; float output's insignificant digits can differ from glibc/MSVC CRT even though round-trip via atof is bit-exact

gotchas: Two open, unresolved correctness/security bugs as of 2026-09-24: stbsp_snprintf(buf, 0, ...) with non-NULL buf writes one byte before the buffer (#1963); large integer precision like "%0.513x" overruns the internal conversion buffer (#1792)
stbsp_set_separators() changes process-wide global state (comma/period), not thread-local or per-call
Float insignificant digits differ from glibc/MSVC CRT output (documented in header) even though round-trip via atof is exact
Several open issues catalog format-flag edge cases (nan/inf capitalization, %A case, negative precision crash) that diverge from strict C sprintf semantics
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The catalogued siblings (Boost.Charconv, c4core, fast_double_parser, rigtorp CharConv, fpconv, double-conversion, milo Grisu2, itoa variants) are narrow number<->string converters that replace std::to_chars/from_chars or a single strtod/itoa call. stb_sprintf is scoped differently: it is a full printf-style format-string engine (mixed text plus args, width/precision, %n, etc.), so pick it when you need a drop-in-shaped replacement for whole sprintf/snprintf call sites -- especially in C or C-style C++ (game/graphics) code that already uses sprintf throughout -- rather than a targeted numeric conversion routine.
verified_claims_summary: The library's own header (stb_sprintf.h, "PERFORMANCE vs MSVC 2008 32-/64-bit") reports first-party speedups against MSVC 2008's CRT sprintf, e.g. %f 7.3x/6.0x faster, %e 8.1x/6.0x, %g 10.0x/7.1x, %d 4.8x/4.0x, and a 512-char string format 35.0x/32.5x faster (32-bit/64-bit builds respectively); no CPU model, optimizer flags, or benchmark harness are given, and GCC's CRT is claimed qualitatively "even slower than MSVC" with no numbers.
status_note: Actively maintained (pushed 2026-08-02, part of the 34.7k-star stb collection, not archived) but has a cluster of open correctness/security issues, including two out-of-bounds-write bugs, unresolved as of 2026-09-24. Dual MIT/public-domain (Unlicense) licensed per the header's own license block, so it is trivially copyable and safe to vendor regardless of upstream fixes.
